title: Chapter 109 – The Garden Hall
html:
[Lin Garden Hall – Lin Wenyuan]

One year later.

Lin Wenyuan has always been a man who makes lists, and on the morning of the charter hearing he makes the longest list of his life.

He does it at the writing desk in the study of the Garden Hall, at the first gray of dawn, with a lamp turned low and a pot of tea at his elbow, in the clear small script of a clerk. It is a habit he formed thirty years ago, as a young man in a failing house, when the only thing he could control was the order in which he worried. He writes the date at the top. Then the headings, in a column, like stakes driven into soft ground.

People. Land. Money. Craft. Enemies.

Under People he writes: 214. Then he stops, and looks at the number, and lets the brush rest.

Two hundred and fourteen souls under one roof, or near it. Seven years ago it was thirty-one, counting the dead. He remembers the night he stood in the cold yard of the old Garden, after the Orchard, with a ledger in his hand and a list of the missing, and thought that he would not live to see another winter. He remembers the weight of the book. He remembers that he had cried.

He writes beneath it, in smaller characters, with the careful pride of a man listing the contents of a treasure chest: Of whom: 61 children. 19 under five. 38 in the Hall school. 12 guards, Foundation-bound. 4 Foundation proper (self, Feng, two cousins). 3 alchemists (Rank 2, 1, 1). 1 artifact refiner (Rank 2). 1 herbalist-apprentice at the Sutra Hall.

Hui, he adds, after a moment. 12. Zhao. Ward of the Hall. Root test today.

He draws a line under it. Beneath Enemies he writes only two entries, because it is early and the tea is hot: The Cloud Peak Hall (courteous). The Office (nameless). He looks at the second for a time. It is a short line. It feels very long.

* * *

The Hall has changed him, and he is not sure he has forgiven it.

He walks the corridors of it at sunrise, with his hands behind his back, as he has done every morning for two years. It is a long timber house on the river bank, built of red-brown pine and gray slate, with deep eaves and a covered walk, and a bell in a little tower over the gate. The bell is rung at dawn and dusk. He rings it himself on the first of each month. It has a plain, kind note, a little cracked, from a bronze that Old Hu cast out of three broken plowshares and the Mu steel that was left.

The common room is already awake. A woman in blue stands at the hearth, stirring a pot, and three children sit cross-legged on the floor with slates in their laps. A man in the corner is mending a harness. A cat sleeps on the warm stones. It smells of porridge and wood smoke and wet wool. Nobody looks up as he passes. They are used to him now. He has become part of the furniture, a thin gray man in an ink-stained robe who goes through the Hall like a draft, touching things.

It is a house, he thinks, with a kind of wonder. We built a house.

At the door of the dispensary he stops.

Qinghe is inside, at the long table, grinding something in a stone bowl, with her sleeves rolled to the elbow and her silver Rank Two pin gleaming at her collar. She does not look up. She has been awake since four. There are shadows under her eyes, but her hands are steady, and the powder that falls from the pestle is fine as flour.

"You did not sleep," she says.

"No more than you."

"I had the better excuse." She taps the bowl. "Three fever cases in the east wing. I wanted them stable before you left." She glances up. "You have your good robe on."

"It's the only one."

"It has a button missing."

He looks down. It does. He had not noticed.

"I will sew it," says his wife, with infinite patience, "while you eat. Sit."

He sits.

* * *

The Zhao family arrives on foot at seven, with a pot of pickled radish and a very large woman.

They come up the river road in a straggling column of forty, in their patched best, with Zhao Yao at the head. He is twenty now, tall and lean, with the burn scar white over one eyebrow and a long cloak of dark blue that is a little too good for him. He carries himself like a man who has been told he is a head of household and has decided, with some reluctance, to believe it. At his side walks Zhao Bei, broad as a barn door, her cropped gray hair freshly washed, with a mattock over her shoulder and a look of cheerful menace.

"We have come to witness," says Yao, bowing. "The Zhao of the Red Ridge. Forty-three. It is what Rong said was needed."

"You are very welcome."

"We have brought radish." Bei sets the pot on the table with a thud. "It is my mother's. It will cure anything, and if it does not, it will convince you that you were not ill."

Wenyuan, who has been trying not to laugh for several minutes, finds that he can no longer help it. Behind him, from the hearth, Old Hu coughs in a way that sounds suspiciously like a snort.

"How is Red Ridge?" he asks.

"Quiet." Yao's face softens. "We have the manor. The fields are planted. The Court sends an inspector twice a year, and he leaves with a hamper and a headache." He hesitates. "My uncle was buried in the spring. On the north slope, beside Lin. We put up a stone. It says both names. Jian came."

"I know. He told me."

"He stood a long time." The young man looks at the floor. "I did not think a man like that would."

"A man like what?"

"A man who is... who has so much to do." Yao lifts his eyes, and they are the same dark steady brown as his uncle's. "I wanted to say it before the hearing. We are Red Ridge Zhao. We have done terrible things, and we are not forgiven. But we do not forget who held the door. If the Court wants a witness, we are forty-three. If it wants a hundred, we will find sixty more."

Wenyuan puts out his hand. After a moment, Yao takes it.

"Welcome to the Hall," says the Patriarch. "Eat. You will have a long day."

Bei looks round at the long common room, the hearth, the benches, the shelf of cubbies. Her small eyes soften.

"It smells like a house," she says to no one in particular. "I had forgotten what that smelled like."

* * *

The clerk comes at eight.

He rides up the river road on a hired mule, in a gray robe and a felt cap, with a canvas satchel strapped to his chest and a smile like a freshly ironed sheet. He dismounts at the gate. He bows to the guard. He is young, perhaps thirty, with an unlined face and neatly oiled hair, and the guard who takes his card does not know why, but he stands up a little straighter.

"Office of Record," says the clerk, in a pleasant tenor. "A routine matter. The Hall's roll, in preparation for the charter hearing."

Wenyuan receives him in the common room, standing, with Feng at his shoulder.

His eldest son has put on weight in the last two years, all of it muscle. Feng wears the silver-edged gray and the Foundation Middle pin, and he stands at the Patriarch's elbow like a gatepost, not touching his sword. He does not need to. The clerk's eyes have gone to him once, assessed, and moved on.

"The Office of Record," Wenyuan repeats. "I was not aware the Court required a countersignature."

"It is a new provision, Patriarch. A courtesy, really." The clerk opens his satchel and lays a sheet on the table: heavy cream paper, ruled in red. "A house seeking charter is expected to lodge its roll with the Sect's Office, for the sake of orderly record. Names, ages, relationships. A copy is returned within the month."

"And what becomes of the original?"

"It is filed."

"Where?"

"In the Office, naturally." The smile is smooth. "I assure you it is a purely formal step."

Wenyuan looks at the paper. At the ruled columns. At the line at the bottom, in a neat clerk's hand, where the head of the house is to sign.

"May I see the Hall's previous filing?" he asks. "The roll we lodged two years ago, at the Court's request?"

A very small silence.

"It will be in the archive."

"Of course. Perhaps you would be so kind as to fetch it." He keeps his voice mild. "I should like to compare the two. I am an old-fashioned man, and I like to see what has become of a thing I have given."

The clerk blinks. "That would take some days."

"I have days."

"The hearing is this afternoon."

"Then I shall sign this afternoon," says Wenyuan gently, "if the previous filing has been produced. And not before."

* * *

His son comes in at ten, from the road.

Wenyuan hears him before he sees him. A footfall on the covered walk, quick and light, with a faint extra beat on the left foot where Jian has favored it since the winter in the mine. A murmur at the gate. A word to the guard. Then the door opens, and there he is: a lean dark young man of twenty-six in a gray tunic and a plain cloak, with his hair tied back and a white jade tag at his throat, standing in the doorway with one hand on the frame.

He looks at the clerk.

It is not a long look. A heartbeat. Two. His eyes go a little out of focus, and his face loses all expression, and something moves behind them, very fast, like a fish turning in deep water. Wenyuan, who has watched his son's face for twenty-six years and has learned to read in it the smallest weather, feels the hair stand up on the back of his neck.

Then the look is gone. Jian smiles. It is a good, ordinary, polite smile.

"Father. Brother. I hope I'm not too late."

"Not at all." Wenyuan rises. "This is the gentleman from the Office of Record. He has brought us a roll."

"How kind." Jian crosses the floor and bows to the clerk, a perfectly correct bow. "I am Lin Jian. I believe we have met in the Hall of Weights."

"I do not recall."

"No. It was a crowd." He turns. "Father. May I have a word?"

They go to the study. It is two paces away, a small room, and the door closes with a click. Wenyuan stands with his back to it, his hands clasped. His son leans against the desk and rubs his eyes.

"Don't sign," says Jian.

"I had not intended to."

"Don't sign anything. Not today. Not with him." His voice is low and quite steady. "I looked at him. I don't know what I saw, exactly. A knot. A cold one. It was tied here," he touches the base of his skull, "and it goes a long way off. He isn't a clerk. He's a hand."

"A Registry hand."

"Yes."

"I thought so. When he said courtesy." Wenyuan sits, heavily, in the chair. He is aware of his own pulse. "What will they do with the roll?"

"Read it. Count it. Find the weak places." Jian's mouth tightens. "Find me. Find Mother. Find anyone who has ever said a word about the cradle."

"No one has."

"No one has. But a roll is a map." He stands, and looks at his father. "Keep your own. Written in your hand, in your house, with the real names. Let the Court have a copy with the dull ones. The Office can have what it likes, as long as it's wrong."

"A false roll."

"A discreet one."

Wenyuan looks at him for a long time.

"You've learned to lie," he says.

"I've learned to count," says his son. "It comes to the same thing."

* * *

The Court Hall of Azure Cloud is a square gray building in the center of the town, with a flat roof and two stone lions at the door, and on the afternoon of the charter hearing it is full.

Wenyuan goes in with his back straight. He has put on the good robe, with the button sewn, and carries a roll of his own in a plain wooden case. He walks between Feng and Old Hu, who has put on a clean shirt and combed his hair and looks so ferocious that the porters step away from him. Behind come Qinghe, in her blue robe and silver pin, and Wenjun with her slate, and a dozen others of the family, and last of all, at a little distance, as though not sure he is invited, a thin dark boy of twelve in a borrowed short robe.

Hui walks with his chin up. He has not let go of the strap of his satchel.

The hearing room is long and high, with a dais at one end and a bench of five Court officials in dark robes. Dai sits on the left, round-faced and smooth, with his jade rings flashing. In the center sits an older man, tall and gray and thin, with the shoulders of a scholar, who rises as the family enters and inclines his head.

Cheng Yun.

He has been restored, then. Wenyuan notes it without surprise. The silver edge on his robe is a full hand wide again. The Examiner of the Hall of Weights has risen to the Court bench, and he regards the Lin clan across the length of the room with that cool, level, scrupulous gaze that Wenyuan remembers from a hundred days in the Garden, a man counting beds and finding every one.

"The petition of the Lin Garden Hall for charter as a minor house of the Sect," Cheng Yun reads. "Petitioner: Lin Wenyuan, Patriarch. Seconded by the Gate Bearer, Lin Jian. Witnessed by the House of Tan, by Zhao Yao of the Red Ridge, and by Deputy Rong of Enforcement." He sets down the paper. "The Court will hear the petitioner."

Wenyuan steps forward.

* * *

He has prepared a speech. It is a good speech. It is fourteen pages long and it begins with the founding of the Garden and ends with the history of the beds, and he has memorized all of it.

He does not give it.

He stands before the bench with his hands at his sides, in the silence of the long room, and finds that the words have gone out of his head like water out of a cracked jar. He sees the five faces. He sees Dai's smooth smile. He sees, at the back, his wife, her hands folded, and his sons, and Old Hu, glowering. He sees the boy with the satchel.

"I am a clerk," he says.

It is not what he meant to say. It comes out in a small plain voice. He hears a rustle behind him.

"I was a clerk. For twenty years. I kept the books of a house that was failing, and I was good at it. I could have told you to the copper how far we had fallen." He pauses. "I did not know how to make a house rise. No one had taught me. I only knew how to count what was lost."

"Patriarch," says Dai, with elaborate patience, "the Court has your petition."

"Yes. I am coming to it." He lifts his eyes. "Seven years ago I had thirty-one people, a failing garden, and a debt. Today I have two hundred and fourteen. Sixty-one are children. Nineteen are under five. Thirty-eight go to our school. I have four Foundation cultivators and three alchemists and a Rank Two artifact refiner. I have a dispensary that treated eight hundred patients last year, and charged for none of the poor." He draws a breath. "I have a granary that has not been empty in five winters. I have a bell. It is cracked. I rang it this morning."

Silence.

"I do not tell you this to boast. I tell you because it is the only argument I have." He lifts the wooden case. "This is the roll of my house. Every name. Every age. Every relation. It is in my own hand. I will lodge it with the Court, and the Court may read it, and verify it, and call any witness it likes. I will not lodge it with the Office of Record."

A murmur runs through the room.

"The Office of Record," says Dai smoothly, "has a long-standing interest in—"

"The Office has had no interest in the Garden for seven years," says Wenyuan, "until a boy of mine walked out of the Dock. I do not say it is a coincidence. I say that a roll is a trust. I have kept mine for thirty years, and I do not intend to give it to a clerk I cannot name."

He sets the case on the Court's table.

"That is my petition," he says. "Thank you."

* * *

Cheng Yun does not rule at once.

He sits for a long time with the case before him, his long fingers resting on the lid. The five officials have turned their heads toward him. In the silence, Wenyuan can hear his own heartbeat, and the creak of the benches, and, from somewhere very far off, the drip of a water-clock.

"The Court notes," says Cheng Yun at last, "that the petition satisfies the conditions of the charter: a membership above one hundred, a head of Foundation rank, a seat within the town, a lawful trade. It notes that the household has been inspected by the Court on twenty-three occasions in seven years, and has been found in good order on each." He lifts his eyes. "It notes also that the Court has, in its own archive, no record of a house of this size that has been so thoroughly honest."

Dai opens his mouth.

"I have not finished, Inspector." The voice is quiet. "The Court will accept the roll as lodged. The Court declines the Office's request for a countersignature, there being no provision in the Rule that requires it." A pause. "The Court is aware of a certain... tendency, in recent years, for provisions to appear which the Rule did not contain. It intends to examine the matter."

The room has gone very still.

"The petition is granted." Cheng Yun inclines his head. "The Lin Garden Hall is chartered as a minor house of the Azure Cloud Sect, under the patronage of the Gate Bearer, with a tribute of one-fifth of its produce and a seat in the Court Hall of the town. The Court congratulates the Patriarch." Something very like a smile crosses his thin face. "And thanks him for the roll."

Behind Wenyuan, a sound goes up that is not quite a cheer. It is a great, long, shuddering exhalation, from forty throats at once, and in the middle of it Qinghe says, quite clearly, "Oh," and sits down on the bench.

He turns.

His wife is laughing. She is sitting on the bench with her silver pin crooked and her hands over her mouth, and tears are running down her face, and Feng has his arm round her, and Old Hu is blowing his nose on a sleeve like a trumpet. Wenjun, in the corner, writes something on her slate with the grim air of a woman recording a miracle. And at the end of the row, a little apart, a thin dark boy in a borrowed short robe is staring at the Court's bench with enormous eyes.

A house, thinks Wenyuan. We have a house.

The price of it will come, he knows. A fifth of the produce. A Gate Bearer's name on every document. A hundred small things he has not yet thought to fear. But for the moment he stands in the gray hall with the sunlight slanting in, and lets himself have it, entire.

* * *

They test Hui at dusk, in the Hall's long room, by the fire.

It is Qinghe's idea. She says that a day like this should end with a beginning, and she takes the old black stone from its box, the same flat saucer of dark glass she has used on every child of the clan for eleven years, and sets it on a cloth on the low table. The family has gathered round. Feng stands behind the Patriarch's chair. Yue, home for the festival, sits cross-legged on the rug with her satchel in her lap. Old Hu leans on the doorpost with his arms folded. Even Wenjun has put down her slate.

The boy stands before the table in his borrowed short robe, with his hands knotted in front of him.

"It does not hurt," says Qinghe gently. "Put your palm flat. Close your eyes. Think of nothing."

"What if there's nothing there?"

"Then there is nothing. And you stay, and we love you, and you learn to read and keep the books." She smiles. "We have a great many people who keep the books. We are very proud of them."

Hui takes a long breath. He sets his hand on the stone.

For a moment, nothing happens.

Then a thread of silver-white light kindles at the center of the dark glass, bright as a needle. It spreads. It runs out in a fine web across the surface of the stone, cold and brilliant, and the room goes quiet. Metal, says Qinghe softly. A second light rises beside it, a warm red-gold, flickering. Fire. The two colors twine, and brighten, and the glass hums.

"Two roots," says Wenyuan, and his throat tightens. "A dual root. A good one."

"Wait," says Yue.

She has risen onto her knees. Her ink-stained fingers are pressed to her mouth. She is staring at the stone, and her eyes are enormous.

A third light has come up.

It is not a color. It is a kind of absence, a pale, clear, cold shimmer at the edge of the glass, like the memory of the moment before snow. It moves through the silver and the gold without touching either. It shivers. It seems almost to look back at them. Then, between one heartbeat and the next, it is gone, and the stone is dark and ordinary, and the boy has taken his hand away.

Nobody speaks.

"What was that?" says Hui, in his small cracked voice. "Did I do something wrong?"

"No," says Qinghe. She has gone pale. "No. You did nothing wrong." She lays a hand on his shoulder, and Wenyuan sees that it is not quite steady. "Metal and fire. That is two. That is very good."

"What was the other?"

"I do not know," says Su Qinghe.

Wenyuan looks at his wife. She looks at him. And in the firelight, in the long room of the house they have built, he sees something pass between them that has not passed in six years, a flicker of old shared fear, as of two people hearing the first footstep on a stair.

A third root, he thinks. The stone has no color for it.

In the corner, Yue says very quietly, to no one: "It looked like the writing on the Gate."
